The author of Ecclesiastes calls himself "the Preacher" (1:1). Some interpreters have concluded that this was Solomon, while others think he was a role-playing writer later than Solomon. Either way, the book claims that its wisdom comes from the "one Shepherd" (12:11), the Lord himself.

The theme of Ecclesiastes is the necessity of fearing God in this fallen, confusing world. Each human being wants to understand all the ways God is acting in the world, but he cannot, because he is not God. And yet the faithful do not despair but cling to God, even when they cannot see what God is doing. The Lord deserves his people's trust. They can leave everything to him while they seek to understand what it means to "fear God and keep his commandments" (12:13). This is true wisdom.
chapter_intro: Fear God, the Holy and Righteous One.

passages.title: Fear God, the Holy and Righteous One.
passages.text: In this section, the encouragement to “fear God” is motivated by his holy and righteous character (compare note on 3:9–15).

passages.title: Life “Under the Sun.”
passages.text: The Preacher observes the hardships of life in a fallen world.

notes.text: People should keep their promises, or vows, to God. By taking a vow, a worshiper would promise to perform a specific act if God would respond favorably to a particular petition.
The political maneuvering of sinful officials results in suffering for the powerless.
The Preacher observes the destructive nature of greed and concludes that a life of contentment is much better (compare Phil. 4:11; 1 Tim. 6:6, 8; Heb. 13:5).
riches were kept . . . to his hurt. A man endured hardship and sacrificed in order to acquire wealth but was never able to enjoy it, because it was lost in a bad venture.
The man’s selfish, fearful greed resulted in a truly wretched life.
he will not much remember . . . his life. The one to whom God grants contentment focuses on blessings from God rather than the darker realities of human existence.
